paragraphs.text: Twice a day along most of the coasts of the world, the sea rises and falls by a distance that can range from a few centimetres to more than fifteen metres. People who lived by the sea noticed long ago that the tides kept time with the moon, arriving about fifty minutes later each day and reaching their greatest range around full and new moon. Explaining why proved much harder than observing it, and a satisfactory account had to wait until the late seventeenth century, when the theory of gravitation provided the necessary tools. Ancient writers recorded the connection, and some suggested that the moon drew the water towards it, which was close to the truth.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The gravity of the moon pulls on the whole Earth, but not equally. The side of the planet facing the moon is closer to it and is pulled slightly more strongly than the centre, while the far side is pulled slightly less. The result is a stretching force that draws water into two bulges, one facing the moon and one on the opposite side. As the Earth rotates beneath these bulges, a given coastline passes through both of them each day, which is why most places experience two high tides and two low tides rather than one. The explanation of the second bulge, on the side facing away from the moon, is the part of the theory that most people find hardest to accept.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The sun produces tides in the same way, but because it is so much further away, its tidal effect is a little less than half that of the moon, despite its enormous mass. When the sun, moon and Earth are in a line, at full and new moon, the two effects combine to produce the large ranges known as spring tides, a name that has nothing to do with the season. When the sun and moon are at right angles to each other, their effects partly cancel, and the smaller neap tides result. Tide tables for ports often mark spring and neap tides because the difference matters greatly to shipping.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: This simple picture explains the rhythm of the tides but not their size or timing at any particular place. If the Earth were covered entirely by deep water, the bulges could follow the moon smoothly; in reality the continents block their path, and the tide behaves more like water sloshing in a series of enormous basins. In each ocean the tide rotates around points, called amphidromic points, where there is almost no rise and fall at all, while the range increases with distance from them. Some coasts, as a result, have only one high tide a day, while others have two of very different heights.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The shape of the coast and the seabed then determines what happens locally. In a long, funnel-shaped bay, the incoming tide is squeezed into an ever narrower space and can rise to extraordinary heights; the largest tidal ranges in the world occur in such places. In some rivers, a rising tide advancing into shallowing water forms a single wave, called a bore, that travels upstream against the current. Such bores have become tourist attractions in several countries, and surfers ride some of them for kilometres. Elsewhere, including parts of the Mediterranean, the range is so small that the tide is scarcely noticed at all.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Tides have a subtle long-term effect on the Earth and the moon. The friction of moving water against the seabed slowly drags on the rotation of the Earth, lengthening the day by a tiny fraction of a second every century. At the same time the moon is gradually moving away from the Earth, by about four centimetres a year, as it gains the energy that the Earth loses. Evidence from ancient growth rings in fossil corals suggests that several hundred million years ago the year contained more than four hundred days. These changes are far too slow to be noticed in a human lifetime, but they are measurable with modern instruments.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Predicting the tides accurately became a matter of great commercial importance as shipping grew. In the nineteenth century, scientists developed methods of breaking the observed tide at a port into a large number of simple components, each linked to a particular movement of the sun or moon. Mechanical machines built from gears and pulleys were then used to combine these components and print tide tables years in advance, a task that was taken over by electronic computers in the second half of the twentieth century. Some of these machines remained in use into the 1960s.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Interest in the tides is now growing for a different reason. Because they are driven by astronomical movements rather than by the weather, tides are entirely predictable, which makes them attractive as a source of electricity. Several schemes use barrages across estuaries or turbines placed in fast tidal currents, although high construction costs and concerns about the effects on wildlife have limited their number. The same regular motion that sailors once had to plan around may yet become a dependable source of power. Tidal energy also has the advantage that its output can be planned years ahead, unlike that of wind or solar power.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: The stripes that run the shop

paragraphs.text: The barcode is so familiar that it has become almost invisible. Few inventions have changed so much while attracting so little attention. Printed on nearly every item sold in a shop, it is scanned billions of times a day and escapes the notice of most customers entirely. Yet the pattern of black and white stripes was the product of decades of experiment, and its adoption required an unusual degree of cooperation among businesses that were otherwise competitors. Its effects have reached far beyond the checkout, changing how goods are ordered, stored and moved around the world.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The idea began with a problem in grocery retailing. In the late 1940s, a grocery executive asked researchers at a technical institute whether there was some way of capturing product information automatically at the checkout. Two graduate students took up the challenge, and one of them, drawing lines in the sand on a beach, is said to have hit on the idea of extending the dots and dashes of Morse code into thick and thin lines. Their patent, granted in the early 1950s, described a pattern of concentric circles that could be read from any direction. The story may have been improved in the retelling, but the inventors themselves confirmed its outline.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The invention was ahead of its time. Reading the pattern required a strong light source and equipment to interpret the reflected light, and the technology of the period made scanners large, expensive and unreliable. The inventors sold their patent, and it expired before the system was ever used commercially. Only with the development of the laser and cheaper electronic circuits in the 1960s did automatic scanning at the checkout become practical, and even then retailers were reluctant to invest until they could be sure that manufacturers would print codes on their products. An early experimental system used by railways to identify freight wagons also failed, because the labels became dirty and could not be read reliably.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The breakthrough was organisational rather than technical. In the early 1970s, a committee of grocery manufacturers and retailers in the United States agreed to adopt a single standard code, choosing a rectangular design of vertical bars submitted by an engineer at a large computer company in preference to several rivals. The standard assigned each product a unique number, with one part identifying the manufacturer and another the individual item. The first product scanned in a shop, in 1974, was a packet of chewing gum, which is now held in a museum. The design was chosen partly because it could be printed reliably on packaging of different materials and could be read even if part of it was damaged. The number printed beneath the bars allows staff to type in the code by hand if the scanner fails.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Adoption was slow at first. Scanners were expensive, and a shop gained little from buying one until most of the products on its shelves carried codes, while manufacturers gained little from printing codes until most shops could read them. Consumer groups also raised concerns that removing individual price labels from items would allow shops to raise prices unnoticed, and some regions passed laws requiring prices to remain on each item for a period. By the early 1980s, however, the number of scanning shops was growing rapidly, and the system soon spread to Europe and beyond. Supporters argued that scanning would reduce errors at the checkout and speed up queues, and studies later confirmed both claims.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The most important consequences were not at the checkout. Because every sale was now recorded automatically, retailers knew precisely which products were selling, where and when, and could reorder stock without counting it by hand. This information shifted power in the supply chain from manufacturers, who had previously known more about demand than shops did, towards large retailers. It also made possible the enormous range of products found in modern supermarkets, since tracking tens of thousands of items by hand would have been impractical. Manufacturers, in turn, began to pay retailers for favourable positions on the shelves, a practice that the data made easier to price.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Barcodes soon spread well beyond food. They are used to track parcels, library books, the medication of hospital patients and luggage at airports, and newer two-dimensional codes, made of small squares rather than lines, can store far more information and be read by the camera of an ordinary phone. In warehouses, codes are increasingly supplemented by radio tags, which can be read without a direct line of sight, although their higher cost has limited their use on low-value items. Some countries also use codes on official documents, from tax forms to boarding passes.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The history of the barcode suggests that the success of a technology often depends less on the invention itself than on the agreements that surround it. The basic idea existed for more than twenty years before it was used, and it succeeded only when competing companies accepted a common standard. The humble stripes on a packet of biscuits are, in that sense, a monument to cooperation as much as to engineering. Many later technologies, from mobile phone networks to the internet itself, followed a similar path, depending on agreed standards as much as on invention.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: Is space exploration worth the money?

paragraphs.text: Every large space mission provokes the same question: could the money not have been better spent on Earth? Government space budgets run to billions a year, and the images of rockets rising while problems of poverty, health and climate remain unsolved give the objection an obvious force. Defenders of space exploration reply that the sums involved are small relative to public spending as a whole and that the benefits, though often indirect, are substantial. Both claims contain some truth, and weighing them requires distinguishing between the different things that space programmes actually do. The debate is old, but the terms in which it is conducted have changed as the costs and the participants have changed.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Much of what is spent on space has little to do with exploration. Rachel Obi, who studies science funding, points out that the largest share of civil and commercial space activity goes on satellites that orbit close to the Earth: those that relay communications, provide positioning signals, observe the weather and monitor crops, forests and ice. These services have become so embedded in daily life that most people are unaware of depending on them. Criticism of space spending, she argues, is usually directed at crewed missions and distant probes, which account for a much smaller part of the total.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The economic case for exploration is often made through the idea of spin-offs, technologies developed for space that later find uses on Earth. Tomasz Nowak, an economist who has examined such claims, is cautious. Some well-known examples turn out on investigation to have been developed elsewhere and merely used by space agencies, and it is difficult to show that the same technologies would not have appeared anyway. He does not deny that space programmes have produced useful innovations, but he argues that spin-offs alone cannot justify the cost, and that a programme should be judged mainly on what it achieves in space. He notes that the most successful examples usually involved close cooperation between space agencies and industry.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Scientific discovery provides a stronger argument. Probes sent to other planets have transformed understanding of how the solar system formed, and telescopes in orbit, free of the distortion caused by the atmosphere, have made observations impossible from the ground. Leila Farah, a planetary scientist, notes that studying other worlds has also improved knowledge of the Earth: the runaway warming of one neighbouring planet and the loss of water on another have informed models of our own climate. For many scientists, this knowledge is valuable in itself, whether or not it produces practical benefits. Some of the most important findings have come from missions that cost less than a single large crewed flight.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Crewed missions are the most expensive and the most contested part of the enterprise. Robots can now carry out much of the work that once required astronauts, at a fraction of the cost and without risk to life. Supporters of human spaceflight argue that people remain far more flexible than machines in unfamiliar conditions, and that the presence of humans generates public interest and political support that robotic missions cannot. Farah accepts the first point for certain kinds of fieldwork but doubts that it justifies the large difference in cost for most scientific purposes. The risk to astronauts also imposes costs of its own, since every system must be designed with a margin of safety that robots do not need.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: A newer argument concerns the long-term future. Some advocates maintain that humanity should become able to live on other worlds as insurance against catastrophe on Earth. Hugo Bernard, who writes on the ethics of technology, regards this argument as weak in its usual form. Any settlement on another planet would depend for generations on supplies from Earth, and the environments available are far harsher than any that a damaged Earth is likely to become. In his view, the resources required would do far more to reduce risks if spent on protecting the planet we already inhabit. He also questions whether the idea receives attention because it is realistic or because it makes an appealing story.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The growth of private companies has changed the terms of the debate. Commercial launch services have reduced the cost of reaching orbit considerably, and private investment now funds activities that once depended entirely on governments. This has not removed public spending, since governments remain the main customers for many of these companies, but it has raised new questions about who controls activity in space and who benefits from it. Obi warns that the growing number of satellites in low orbit risks crowding and collisions if international rules do not keep pace. The same companies have announced plans for tourism in space, which raises further questions about the purpose of the activity.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Whether space exploration is worth the money depends on which part of it is being discussed. Satellites that serve daily needs are among the most useful investments any society makes; robotic science offers valuable knowledge at moderate cost; crewed missions and plans for settlement are harder to justify on practical grounds and rest largely on arguments about inspiration and the long-term future. Treating all of these as a single expense, to be accepted or rejected as a whole, obscures more than it reveals.
paragraphs.label: H
